title: The Night the Stars Fell: 12–13 November 1833
subtitle: The great Leonid meteor storm over North America, with its 1799 forerunner and its 1866–67 explanation
intro: In the last hours before dawn on Wednesday 13 November 1833, the sky over most of North America filled with meteors. From New England to the Gulf, and west across the Mississippi to the Plains, people woke to a sky in which streaks of light fell faster than anyone could count, for two or three hours, until daylight drowned them. Modern estimates put the rate in the tens of thousands per hour. The night was clear and cold almost everywhere, so almost everyone east of the Rockies who was awake, or was woken, saw the same thing at the same moment.

What they made of it depended on who they were. In New Haven the Yale professor Denison Olmsted noticed that the meteors seemed to stream from one point among the stars of Leo, and that the point moved with the stars, not with the Earth. He asked the public, through the newspapers, to send him their observations, and turned what came back into the first long scientific study of a meteor shower. In Kirtland, Ohio, Joseph Smith wrote in his journal that the falling stars fulfilled scripture. On the Eastern Shore of Maryland a fifteen-year-old enslaved boy, Frederick Bailey, later Frederick Douglass, watched at daybreak and wondered if the Son of Man was coming. On the bank of the Missouri, Latter-day Saint families just driven out of Jackson County took the sky as a sign in their favour. On the northern Plains, Lakota and Nakota keepers of winter counts gave the whole winter of 1833–34 its name from the night.

The record is mixed, and the form tags say so. Smith's journal entry was written within days. The newspapers were printed within a week or two. Olmsted's and Alexander Twining's papers in the American Journal of Science appeared in 1834. Douglass's account was written twenty-two years later, in his 1855 memoir, and Parley Pratt's in an autobiography published in 1874. The winter counts are pictographic records dated by winter rather than by day, recorded by Garrick Mallery and other collectors decades later. Testimonies of formerly enslaved people collected by the WPA in the 1930s, and an anecdote that Abraham Lincoln, then in Illinois, later retold the night during the Civil War (it reaches us second-hand, through Walt Whitman), are a full century or a generation removed and are not used here as entries.

The night had a forerunner. On 12 November 1799 Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland at Cumaná, on the coast of what is now Venezuela, and the American surveyor Andrew Ellicott, at sea off the Florida Keys, saw the same kind of storm. In 1833 a North Carolina paper reprinted a description of the Cumaná display beside its own. Thirty-one years later Hubert Anson Newton of Yale, working through old chronicles, found the storms returned about every thirty-three years and predicted one for November 1866. It came, over Europe. Early in 1867 Giovanni Schiaparelli and others showed that the meteors travel in the orbit of a comet found in 1865–66 by Wilhelm Tempel and Horace Tuttle. The falling stars were the debris of a comet.

The chapter is built around the single night of 13 November 1833, laid out from east to west, and the explaining that came after: newspaper theories of frost, miasma, electricity and phosphorus; Olmsted's nebulous cloud circling the Sun; and finally the comet. Olmsted's own first word on the cause, that it was not yet explained, is the honest centre of the story.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and need no conversion. The storm is usually dated to the night of 12–13 November 1833, with the peak in the early morning of Wednesday 13 November (about 4–5 a.m. in the eastern states, earlier by the clock further west). Humboldt dated the 1799 display to the night of 11–12 November; its peak fell in the early morning of 12 November. Plains winter counts name a whole winter (roughly first snow to spring), so the 1833–34 entries are placed at November 1833 by convention, with precision 'year'. Memoirs written long after are placed on the night they describe but tagged as later recollections.

eyes.name: Denison Olmsted
eyes.role: Professor of mathematics and natural philosophy at Yale College, aged 42
eyes.side: United States; Yale and Silliman's American Journal of Science
eyes.vantage_label: the scientist who turned the night into data
eyes.form: newspaper letter and published scientific papers
eyes.authenticity: His newspaper notice was reprinted widely in November 1833. His two-part 'Observations on the Meteors of November 13th, 1833' appeared in the American Journal of Science in 1834 (part I in the January number, from p. 363 of vol. 25). He returned to the subject in an 1838 paper on the November shower of 1837 and in his Letters on Astronomy (1840).
eyes.bio: Olmsted was woken by a neighbour and watched the end of the storm in New Haven. His appeal for reports made the 1833 storm an early case of the public collecting data for a scientist, and his papers established that the meteors came from beyond the atmosphere and radiated from a point in Leo. His own theory of a nebulous cloud circling the Sun was later abandoned, but the radiant and the cosmic origin stood.

sources.title: Excerpts with citation of Olmsted, AJS Jan. 1834, p. 363
Sketch of Denison Olmsted, Popular Science Monthly vol. 46
J. R. Eastman, The Progress of Meteoric Astronomy in America (1890)

eyes.name: Alexander Catlin Twining
eyes.authenticity: His 'Investigations respecting the Meteors of Nov. 13th, 1833' appeared in the American Journal of Science in July 1834 (vol. 26). Exactly where he stood that night is not fixed in the sources consulted; he is described in the period literature as 'of West Point'.
eyes.bio: Twining worked through the reports independently of Olmsted and reached a similar conclusion: the meteors came from a fixed point among the stars and so from outside the atmosphere. He stayed with meteors for decades, later writing on the August shower and on meteoric rings.

sources.title: Excerpts with citation of Twining, AJS July 1834
Sketch of Denison Olmsted (names Twining of West Point)

eyes.name: Boston Evening Transcript (editors and correspondents)
eyes.vantage_label: city newspaper on the morning itself
eyes.authenticity: Quoted in Mark Littmann, The Heavens on Fire (1998), and in the Smithsonian Magazine account; the original issue was not consulted directly.
eyes.bio: Boston's evening paper printed its account on the day of the storm itself. Its phrasing is among the most often repeated: a sky in which meteors came too fast to count.

sources.title: Leonid quotations (Littmann extracts)
Smithsonian Magazine, 2024

eyes.name: Frederick Douglass (then Frederick Bailey)
eyes.role: Enslaved youth, about 15, in the household of Thomas Auld
eyes.authenticity: Written in My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), twenty-two years after the night, and retold in Life and Times (1881). The memory is consistent with the date: he says he had moved from Baltimore to St. Michael's in March 1833.
eyes.bio: Douglass placed the falling stars in the darkest year of his youth, after he was taken from Baltimore to St. Michael's. He read the sky through the scripture he had taught himself to read, and wrote of it as a possible sign of deliverance. His is the best-known Black eyewitness account of the night.

sources.title: My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), page with the meteor passage
Project Gutenberg text

eyes.name: Tarborough Southerner (editors)
eyes.authenticity: Issue of 22 November 1833, page 2, digitised by DigitalNC; the OCR is partly garbled.
eyes.bio: A week after the storm the Tarboro weekly printed its townspeople's account and a sheaf of reprints from Newbern, Richmond and Norfolk papers, each with a theory, and an old description of the 1799 display at Cumaná. The page shows a small-town press doing its best to explain the sky.

sources.title: Tarborough Southerner, 22 Nov. 1833, p. 2 (DigitalNC)

eyes.name: Joseph Smith Jr.
eyes.role: Founding prophet of the Church of Christ (Latter Day Saints), aged 27
eyes.authenticity: Journal, 1832–1834, in his own hand for the 13 November entry (earlier entries in Oliver Cowdery's hand); edited by the Joseph Smith Papers. A reworded version entered his later History and was printed in Times and Seasons in 1845.
eyes.bio: Smith had just come home from a missionary journey to Upper Canada when a fellow member knocked at his door before dawn. He wrote the night up as a literal fulfilment of scripture and a sign of the nearness of Christ's coming. His entry is one of the few true diary records of the storm.

sources.title: Journal, 1832–1834, p. 18 (Joseph Smith Papers)
Sign of Christ's Second Coming (JSP event)

eyes.name: Sangamo Journal (editors)
eyes.authenticity: Issue of 16 November 1833, as quoted in a local-history compilation; the original issue was not consulted directly.
eyes.bio: Springfield's weekly reported the storm three days later. It stands in for the Mississippi Valley, where the storm was seen just as fully as on the coast.

sources.title: Logan County (Illinois) accounts, quoting the Sangamo Journal

eyes.name: Parley Parker Pratt
eyes.role: Latter-day Saint apostle-to-be and missionary, aged 26
eyes.side: Latter-day Saints expelled from Jackson County, Missouri
eyes.where: Camp on the Missouri River bottoms, between Jackson and Clay counties, Missouri
eyes.authenticity: Autobiography of Parley Parker Pratt, published posthumously in 1874; written years after the event. Some details are placed loosely in time.
eyes.bio: Pratt was among the Saints driven out of Jackson County in early November 1833, camping on the river bottoms in the cold. To the refugees, and by their account to some of their enemies, the falling stars looked like a heavenly judgment. His version is the camp's.

sources.title: KSL account quoting Pratt's Autobiography

eyes.name: Lone Dog (Shunka-ishnala), winter-count keeper
eyes.role: Keeper of a Yanktonai winter count covering 1800–1871
eyes.where: Upper Missouri country (the count was later reported from near Fort Peck, Montana)
eyes.form: winter count (pictographic calendar, dated by winter)
eyes.authenticity: The original hide is not known to survive; copies, including a painted muslin at the Buffalo Bill Center of the West, and Mallery's published transcriptions (1877, 1886, 1893) carry it. The keeper's location in 1833 is not exactly known.
eyes.bio: Lone Dog's count marks each winter with one picture. For 1833–34 it shows a dark moon or disk among falling stars. Ethnologists later used this winter to line up Plains calendars with the Western calendar, because so many counts mark it.

sources.title: Symbols in Lone Dog's Winter Count (after Mallery 1893)
Lakota winter counts as counter-archives

eyes.name: Battiste Good (Wapóštaŋǧi Máza / Brown Hat)
eyes.role: Sicangu Lakota; aged about 12 in 1833, later a band leader and keeper of a winter count
eyes.where: Sicangu range, upper Missouri–Platte country (exact camp not known)
eyes.form: winter count (pictographic calendar, dated by winter)
eyes.authenticity: Copies held by the Indian Arts and Crafts Board (Sioux Indian Museum) and the National Anthropological Archives; published by Mallery. The 1833–34 picture was drawn, or redrawn, decades after the winter it names.
eyes.bio: Battiste Good's count, one of the best documented, gives 1833–34 a tipi in a field of stars. He was a boy that winter; the count is his people's memory rather than a diary.

sources.title: Treasures of the IACB: Battiste Good, Lakota winter counts

eyes.name: Alexander von Humboldt
eyes.role: Prussian naturalist-explorer, aged 30, with the botanist Aimé Bonpland
eyes.authenticity: Described in the Relation historique (Personal Narrative), published from 1814; his field diaries survive in Berlin. Bonpland saw the display first.
eyes.bio: Humboldt's account of the 1799 storm became the standard description, and was in circulation when the 1833 storm came. He also gathered reports of the same night from Greenland, Labrador and Germany, the first sign that such a display could be seen across hemispheres.

sources.title: Leonid observations over the last millennium (Cambridge)

eyes.name: Andrew Ellicott
eyes.role: US surveyor returning from the southern boundary survey, aged 45
eyes.where: Aboard ship off the Florida Keys
eyes.authenticity: Published in The Journal of Andrew Ellicott (Philadelphia, 1803) and noticed by the American Philosophical Society; the wording here is taken from a secondary compilation.
eyes.bio: Ellicott was sailing home from surveying the boundary with Spanish Florida when he was called on deck to see the 1799 storm. His is the American record of the forerunner night.

sources.title: Leonid quotations (Ellicott extract)

eyes.name: Hubert Anson Newton
eyes.vantage_label: the historian who predicted the return
eyes.authenticity: His 1864 papers in the American Journal of Science on the old accounts of the November star-shower are well documented; the details here rest on secondary histories.
eyes.bio: Newton gathered descriptions of earlier November storms from chronicles back to AD 902 and found a cycle of about 33 years. He predicted a return in November 1866, and his prediction and his orbit work prepared the way for the comet link.

sources.title: AMS: early years of meteor observation in the USA
Eastman 1890

eyes.name: Giovanni Virginio Schiaparelli
eyes.role: Astronomer at the Brera Observatory, aged 31
eyes.authenticity: His letters of 1866 to Angelo Secchi and his papers of 1866–67 are published; the 1871 German edition collected them. Exact dates here rest on secondary histories.
eyes.bio: Schiaparelli showed that the August Perseids follow the orbit of a comet seen in 1862, and then that the November Leonids follow the orbit of the comet found in 1865–66 by Tempel and Tuttle. He turned the falling stars of 1833 from a cloud of unknown nature into a comet's trail.

sources.title: Leonid observations over the last millennium (Cambridge)

entries.headline: An earthquake shakes Cumaná a week before the stars fall
entries.digest: Humboldt and Bonpland felt their first earthquake in the New World at Cumaná. Humboldt wrote at length about how the shock undid his sense of the ground as solid, and how the townspeople watched the sky afterwards for signs. A week later the sky gave them one.
entries.source_note: Humboldt, Personal Narrative, the Cumaná chapters; date as usually given

entries.date_display: Night of 11–12 November 1799, from about 2.30 a.m.
entries.headline: Bonpland, up for cool air, sees the eastern sky burning
entries.digest: Bonpland had risen in the small hours to enjoy the cool on the gallery and was the first to see it: luminous meteors pouring across the east. Humboldt joined him and they watched thousands of fireballs and shooting stars for about four hours, until sunrise, many leaving bright trails. Humboldt noted the sky was clear and the air calm.
entries.source_note: Humboldt, Personal Narrative; Leonid history in Cambridge Highlights of Astronomy

entries.headline: Old people of Cumaná remember an earlier sky and an earthquake
entries.digest: Humboldt recorded that older inhabitants linked the display with one they remembered before the great earthquake of 1766, and that many of the townspeople read the falling stars as connected with the recent earthquake. He set down their belief beside his own careful timings.
entries.source_note: Humboldt, Personal Narrative (recollection of the 1766 earthquake as he reports it)

entries.place: At sea off the Florida Keys
entries.headline: Ellicott is called on deck to see the shooting stars
entries.digest: Sailing home from the Florida boundary survey, Ellicott was woken around two in the morning to see the sky filled with meteors in every direction. He described a display that seemed to go on without pause until daylight, and compared it with fireworks, but grander.
entries.quote: I was called up to see the shooting stars
entries.source_note: Journal of Andrew Ellicott (1803), as quoted in Littmann's compilation (todayinsci.com)

entries.headline: Ellicott's journal goes into print with the meteor night
entries.digest: The meteor storm entered print in Ellicott's published journal of the boundary survey. It became, with Humboldt's account, the record that men of 1833 would turn to when they asked whether such a thing had happened before.
entries.source_note: The Journal of Andrew Ellicott (Philadelphia, 1803)

entries.headline: Humboldt publishes the Cumaná night and the far reports
entries.digest: In the narrative of his travels Humboldt described the Cumaná storm and added reports that the same night had been seen by Moravian missionaries in Labrador and Greenland and by observers in Germany. He drew the conclusion that the display had covered an enormous area, a first hint that it came from far above the Earth.
entries.source_note: Humboldt, Relation historique / Personal Narrative; publication spread over 1814–1825

entries.headline: Taken from Baltimore to St. Michael's
entries.digest: Frederick, about fifteen, was sent from Baltimore, where he had learned to read, to the household of Thomas Auld at St. Michael's on the Eastern Shore. He later described the change as a fall into hunger and harshness, and placed the falling stars in this same year.
entries.source_note: My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), page with the move and the meteor passage

entries.headline: Driven from Jackson County to the river bottoms
entries.digest: Armed mobs drove the Latter-day Saints out of Jackson County in the first days of November. Pratt and hundreds of others crossed or camped along the Missouri River bottoms in rain and cold, cutting cottonwoods for rough shelters. Letters to Kirtland from Missouri leaders called it a horrible time.
entries.source_note: Pratt, Autobiography (1874), and KSL account quoting Pratt and W. W. Phelps

entries.headline: Lone Dog's count names the winter for the meteors
entries.digest: Lone Dog's count gives the winter of 1833–34 a single picture: a dark moon or disk with stars around it, glossed by later collectors as the meteor shower, or the stars falling. On a calendar with one image per year, the night outweighed every hunt, battle and treaty of that winter.
entries.source_note: Lone Dog winter count, after Mallery (1893), Picture-Writing of the American Indians, pp. 266–87

entries.headline: A tipi in a field of stars
entries.digest: Battiste Good's count shows the winter as a tipi covered and surrounded by stars. He was about twelve. The image belongs to the many Lakota counts that remember 1833–34 as the year the stars fell; others in Smithsonian collections, including American Horse's, mark it too.
entries.source_note: Treasures of the IACB: Battiste Good winter counts

entries.headline: Home from Canada, finding the family well
entries.digest: After a missionary trip to Upper Canada, Smith left Buffalo on 1 November and reached Kirtland on the 4th. His journal, in Oliver Cowdery's hand for these days, gives thanks that he found his family well. The entry for the next nine days is blank: nothing worth noting happened.
entries.source_note: Journal, 1832–1834, p. 18 (Joseph Smith Papers)

entries.headline: Boston: meteors too fast to count
entries.digest: Boston's evening paper reported the morning's display the same day. It described meteor following meteor so quickly that counting was hopeless, and another Boston account spoke of a war of shooting stars in the northwest. Watchmen and early risers had woken neighbours to see it.
entries.source_note: Boston Evening Transcript, 13 Nov. 1833, quoted in Littmann and in Smithsonian Magazine

entries.headline: Woken by a neighbour, Olmsted sees the point in Leo
entries.digest: Olmsted was called out of bed by a neighbour and watched the last part of the storm. He saw that the trails, traced backwards, met at one point in the sky, and that this point stayed fixed among the stars of Leo as the sky turned, rather than staying overhead. That single observation told him the meteors came from beyond the atmosphere.
entries.quote: observed it to be in the constellation Leo
entries.source_note: Olmsted's account as quoted in Smithsonian Magazine; AMS history; Popular Science Monthly sketch

entries.headline: Twining watches the storm on the Hudson
entries.digest: Twining saw the storm in the Hudson valley and began collecting his own reports. His later paper called it a rare and wonderful display, and treated it as a problem in geometry: where did the paths converge, and how high did the meteors light up?
entries.source_note: Twining, AJS July 1834; place from period description 'of West Point'

entries.headline: An enslaved boy sees the stars fall and thinks of deliverance
entries.digest: Douglass saw the storm at about daybreak and remembered being struck with awe. The air seemed full of bright messengers falling from the sky. He had read that the stars would fall before the Son of Man came, and was half ready to welcome Christ as a friend and deliverer, because in that year he was in great distress of mind.
entries.quote: I witnessed this gorgeous spectacle, and was awe-struck
entries.source_note: My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), p. 186 (written 22 years later)

entries.headline: Woken at four: the stars fall like hail
entries.digest: At four in the morning Brother Davis knocked at Smith's door, calling him to come and see the signs in the heavens. Smith went out and saw the stars falling thick, and wrote that it was a literal fulfilment of the word of God and a sure sign that Christ's coming was near. He wrote in his own hand, joyfully, not in fear.
entries.source_note: Journal, 1832–1834, entry of 13 Nov. 1833 (Joseph Smith Papers)

entries.headline: Springfield wakes to myriads of meteors
entries.digest: The Springfield weekly reported that from about three in the morning a shower of countless meteors or shooting stars fell across the sky. Local pioneers later remembered that some people thought the end of the world had come.
entries.quote: the falling of myriads of meteors or shooting stars
entries.source_note: Sangamo Journal, 16 Nov. 1833, as quoted in a Logan County history compilation

entries.headline: Refugees in the river bottoms woken by a cry of signs
entries.digest: In the refugee camp, Pratt recalled, people were woken in the small hours by the cry of signs in the heavens. The meteors fell like splendid fireworks for hours. The exiles took them as a sign that God had not forgotten them, and Pratt later wrote that some of their persecutors were frightened.
entries.quote: the cry of signs in the heavens
entries.source_note: Pratt, Autobiography (1874), as quoted by KSL; written decades later

entries.headline: Boston watchers note the meteors' common origin
entries.digest: Boston accounts, like those Olmsted collected, said the meteors seemed to start from the same region of the sky and fall outward in every direction. Lay witnesses without instruments had seen the radiant the professors would measure.
entries.source_note: Boston reports as summarised in Littmann and Smithsonian Magazine

entries.headline: Olmsted asks the public for reports
entries.digest: Olmsted sent a notice to the New Haven paper describing what he had seen and asking anyone who had watched the storm to send times, directions and details. Papers across the country reprinted it. On the cause he was careful: no one had yet explained it, and the electrical theories in the press did not persuade him.
entries.quote: I do not consider it as hitherto explained
entries.source_note: Olmsted's newspaper letter as quoted in Smithsonian Magazine; AMS history; exact paper and date not confirmed

entries.headline: Illinois prints its account three days on
entries.digest: The Sangamo Journal's report, printed the Saturday after, joined a chorus of western papers. Accounts from the Mississippi valley matched those from the coast in the hour of the peak, which mattered to Olmsted: the same meteors were seen at once from places hundreds of miles apart.
entries.source_note: Sangamo Journal, 16 Nov. 1833, as quoted in a local history compilation

entries.headline: Tarboro: a singular and sublime phenomenon
entries.digest: The Tarboro editors reported that many townspeople saw luminous points fall for an hour or more in great profusion. On the Tuesday night, they said, the thermometer had dropped about 25 degrees around the start of the display. They noted that nobody found any dust or residue the next day, and so preferred the name shooting stars to a shower of fire.
entries.source_note: Tarborough Southerner, 22 Nov. 1833, p. 2 (DigitalNC)

entries.headline: Theories from Newbern, Richmond and Norfolk
entries.digest: The same page reprinted other papers' explanations. The Newbern Spectator placed the shower between three o'clock and daylight. The Richmond Whig blamed frost-killed vegetation releasing a miasma, with electricity acting to purify the air. The Norfolk Herald wrote of phosphoric matter igniting above the clouds and noted that no harm had been done.
entries.source_note: Tarborough Southerner, 22 Nov. 1833, p. 2 (DigitalNC; OCR partly garbled)

entries.headline: An 1799 description from Cumaná reprinted beside 1833
entries.digest: The page also carried, through the Newbern Spectator, a description of the 12 November 1799 display at Cumaná, called grand and awful, with meteors flying in every direction. Thirty-four years apart, the two November nights were already set side by side in a small Carolina weekly.
entries.source_note: Tarborough Southerner, 22 Nov. 1833, p. 2 (DigitalNC)

entries.headline: Letters pour in to Yale
entries.digest: Through late November and December reports reached Olmsted from across the eastern half of the continent: from professors, ship captains, planters and townspeople. They agreed on the hour, the clear cold sky and the radiant point, and gave him the material for a long analysis.
entries.source_note: AMS history; Olmsted, AJS 1834

entries.headline: Part one in Silliman's journal: the greatest display on record
entries.digest: Olmsted's 'Observations on the Meteors of November 13th, 1833' opened in the January number of the American Journal of Science. He called it probably the most extensive and magnificent display of shooting stars ever recorded, and laid out the reports, the timings and the radiant.
entries.source_note: Olmsted, AJS vol. 25 (Jan. 1834), p. 363, as cited

entries.headline: Part two: a nebulous cloud circling the Sun
entries.digest: In the second part Olmsted argued that the meteors fell from a point about 2,238 miles up, entered the air at about four miles a second, and were light combustible matter that burned out. He proposed they were the outer parts of a nebulous body orbiting the Sun inside the Earth's orbit, with a period of about 182 days, met by the Earth each November.
entries.source_note: Eastman (1890) summary of Olmsted, AJS vol. 26 (1834)

entries.headline: Twining's investigations: a rare and wonderful display
entries.digest: Twining's paper treated the meteors as bodies coming from a fixed direction in space, and calculated heights and paths from paired observations. He wrote of the rare and wonderful display and of its terrible magnitude, and agreed with Olmsted that the source lay far outside the atmosphere.
entries.source_note: Twining, AJS vol. 26 (July 1834), pp. 337, 351, as cited

entries.headline: Olmsted organises students to watch the November sky
entries.digest: Hoping for a return, Olmsted organised watches in November 1837 with students and amateurs and published the results in 1838. The rates were nothing like 1833, but the habit of an organised November watch had begun.
entries.source_note: Olmsted, 'On the Meteoric Shower of November, 1837', AJS 33 (1838), pp. 379–93 (AMS history)

entries.headline: The storm in a popular astronomy book
entries.digest: In his Letters on Astronomy, written for general readers, Olmsted retold the storm and his explanation. The night had become a textbook case of how a sky event could be studied with many people's reports.
entries.source_note: Olmsted, Letters on Astronomy (1840 ed.), pp. 348–49, as cited

entries.headline: Douglass writes the night into his second autobiography
entries.digest: In My Bondage and My Freedom Douglass set the falling stars in the year of his removal to St. Michael's. The passage joins the sign to his own state of mind: a youth whose every attachment had been broken, looking up for a deliverer.
entries.source_note: My Bondage and My Freedom (1855)

entries.headline: Newton reads the chronicles and finds a 33-year cycle
entries.digest: Newton gathered accounts of November meteor storms from chronicles reaching back to AD 902, including 1799 and 1833. He found they returned roughly every 33¼ years, worked out possible orbits, and predicted a strong return about 13–14 November 1866.
entries.source_note: Newton, AJS 1864, via AMS and Cambridge Leonid histories

entries.headline: The prediction comes true, over Europe
entries.digest: The storm returned on schedule but at an hour that favoured Europe, where observers counted thousands per hour. In America the display was weaker. Newton's prediction was taken as confirmed, and attention turned to the meteors' orbit.
entries.source_note: AMS history; Cambridge Leonid history

entries.headline: Letters to Secchi: meteors follow comets
entries.digest: In letters to the Jesuit astronomer Angelo Secchi, Schiaparelli argued that the August meteors travel in the orbit of the comet of 1862 (Swift–Tuttle). If one shower followed a comet, others might.
entries.source_note: Schiaparelli's 1866 letters to Secchi, as summarised in Leonid histories

entries.headline: The November meteors share a comet's orbit
entries.digest: With orbital elements for the Leonids now computed (by Le Verrier and others), Schiaparelli noted that they matched the orbit of comet 1866 I, found by Tempel in December 1865 and by Tuttle in January 1866, as computed by Oppolzer. C. F. Peters reached the same match independently. The meteors of 1799 and 1833 were the debris of a comet with a period of about 33 years.
entries.source_note: Leonid histories (Cambridge Highlights of Astronomy); exact dates of the papers not confirmed

entries.headline: A theory of shooting stars, collected
entries.digest: Schiaparelli's papers were collected in a German edition as a sketch of an astronomical theory of shooting stars. It fixed the view that meteor showers are comet debris met by the Earth at the same point of its orbit each year.
entries.source_note: Schiaparelli, Entwurf einer astronomischen Theorie der Sternschnuppen (1871)

entries.headline: Pratt's memoir published, with the river-bottom night
entries.digest: Pratt's autobiography, edited by his son and published in 1874, put the Missouri camp's night into print. It joined a growing body of Latter-day Saint accounts that read the storm as a sign tied to the expulsion from Jackson County.
entries.source_note: Autobiography of Parley Parker Pratt (1874)

entries.headline: Douglass tells the night again, nearly fifty years on
entries.digest: In Life and Times of Frederick Douglass he retold the falling stars of 1833 in much the same terms. By then the scientists had their comet; Douglass kept his meaning, a sign seen by a boy in bondage.
entries.source_note: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881), as cited in later compilations

claims.claim: Cumaná: thousands of fireballs and shooting stars in the east for about four hours, until sunrise; seen first by Bonpland
Off the Florida Keys: called up at about 2 a.m. to see meteors in all directions until daylight
claims.evidence: Journal of Andrew Ellicott (1803), as quoted

claims.claim: Same night reported from Labrador, Greenland and Germany: display covered an immense area
Kirtland: stars falling thick at 4 a.m.; read as a literal fulfilment of scripture and sign of Christ's coming
New Haven: trails converge on a radiant that stays fixed among the stars of Leo as the sky turns
Boston: meteors in such rapid succession they could not be counted
claims.evidence: Boston Evening Transcript, 13 Nov. 1833 (quoted by Littmann)

claims.claim: St. Michael's, Maryland: storm at daybreak, read as a possible sign of the Son of Man's coming
Springfield, Illinois: myriads of meteors from about 3 a.m.
Cause 'not hitherto explained'; electrical explanations rejected
claims.evidence: Olmsted's newspaper letter (quoted in Smithsonian Magazine)

claims.claim: Tarboro: falls for an hour or more; thermometer down about 25 degrees at the start; no dust found next day
Rival theories reprinted: frost-killed vegetation and miasma with electricity (Richmond Whig); phosphoric fluid igniting above the clouds (Norfolk Herald)
Yanktonai count names the whole winter for the meteor storm (dark disk among stars)
claims.evidence: Lone Dog winter count, after Mallery 1893

claims.claim: Meteors from about 2,238 miles up at about 4 miles per second; a nebulous body orbiting the Sun with period about 182 days
Fixed radiant in space shows origin far beyond the atmosphere; heights computed from paired observations
November storms recur about every 33¼ years since AD 902; return predicted for 13–14 Nov. 1866
Leonid orbit matches comet 1866 I (Tempel–Tuttle), period about 33 years; match found independently by Peters

convergences.label: The forerunner night, 1799
convergences.note: Humboldt on a gallery in Cumaná and Ellicott at sea off Florida, some 2,500 km apart, were woken at nearly the same hour. Humboldt timed it and collected far reports; Ellicott compared it to fireworks. Neither knew the other was watching.

convergences.label: Before dawn on the Atlantic seaboard
convergences.note: From Boston to the Eastern Shore of Maryland, a newspaper, two scientists and an enslaved boy saw the same storm within the same hour. The scientists traced the paths back to Leo; the Boston paper gave up counting; Douglass thought of scripture and deliverance.

convergences.label: The same hour inland: Ohio, Illinois, Missouri
convergences.note: In Kirtland, Smith wrote of joy and fulfilled prophecy; in Springfield, the paper reported myriads of meteors; on the Missouri the expelled Saints took it as a sign for them. West of the Appalachians the storm came earlier by the clock but at the same instant.

convergences.label: The Plains name the winter
convergences.note: Where no one wrote dated diaries, keepers of winter counts gave the whole winter of 1833–34 the falling stars as its one image. The same night later let ethnologists anchor Plains calendars to the Western one.

convergences.label: The week of explanations
convergences.note: Within ten days the press offered frost and miasma, electricity and phosphorus; Olmsted said plainly it was not yet explained and asked for data. The Tarboro page even set the 1799 Cumaná account beside the new one.

convergences.label: The two papers in Silliman's journal
convergences.note: Working from the same pool of reports, Olmsted and Twining both fixed the meteors' origin beyond the atmosphere. Olmsted's cloud with a six-month orbit was soon abandoned; the radiant was not.

convergences.label: The return and the comet
convergences.note: Newton's prediction from old chronicles came true over Europe; within weeks Schiaparelli and Peters tied the stream to the comet of Tempel and Tuttle, explaining the night of 1833 a generation after it.

ties.note: Both analysed the 1833 storm in the American Journal of Science in 1834, from overlapping sets of reports, and reached similar conclusions about the radiant.
Olmsted's appeal circulated through newspapers like Boston's, and newspaper reports were among the material he analysed.
Humboldt's account of the 1799 Cumaná storm was the standard precedent that American writers of 1833–34 compared with the new display.
The Tarborough Southerner reprinted a description of the 12 November 1799 Cumaná display beside its 1833 account.
Ellicott's shipboard sighting off Florida became one of the far reports of the same 1799 night, set beside Humboldt's in later histories.
Newton taught at Yale, where Olmsted had built the 1833 study; Olmsted's reports were part of the record from which Newton derived the 33-year cycle.
Newton's 1864 list of past storms included 1799, the night Humboldt described, as a key step in the cycle.
Schiaparelli's comet link built on the orbital work that followed Newton's prediction; Newton wrote on Schiaparelli's theory in 1867.
Not kin, but fellow leaders of the same church: Smith in Ohio and Pratt in Missouri read the same night as a sign, 1,100 km apart, Pratt for the expelled Missouri Saints.
Both counts were transcribed and published by Garrick Mallery, who used the 1833–34 star winter to align them with each other and with the Western calendar.

threads_out.note: Humboldt's description of the 12 November 1799 storm at Cumaná, during the travels told in that chapter, was the precedent newspapers and scientists reached for in 1833.

The 1866–67 proof that meteor showers are comet debris changed what a comet meant; by 1910 the public could fear Earth passing through the tail of Halley's comet in terms the Leonid work had made familiar.

The same American Journal of Science and the same habit of collecting dispersed public reports carried both stories; in 1833 Hitchcock even suggested the meteors were a form of aurora, the phenomenon that dominates the 1859 chapter.
